items.q: Machine Learning is best defined as systems that:
options: Follow explicit hand-written rules for every case
Learn automatically from data and improve with experience without explicit programming
items.explain: ML is a branch of AI where systems learn from data patterns instead of explicit instructions, improving with experience.

items.q: Using AI tools (like Copilot) to improve software-engineering tasks is called:
items.explain: AI4SE = AI *for* Software Engineering (AI tools improving SE tasks). SE4AI = applying SE principles to build reliable AI systems.

items.q: A key contrast between ML and traditional SE is that ML output is:
items.explain: SE produces predictable, deterministic code; ML produces a probabilistic, data-driven model. ML is data-driven, SE is process-driven.

items.q: According to the key takeaways, when using AI in software engineering:
options: Human oversight is non-negotiable — every AI suggestion must be validated
Developers no longer need engineering fundamentals
items.explain: The SDLC still governs the process; AI accelerates subtasks but human oversight is non-negotiable — engineers must validate AI output. You need new skills, not new fundamentals.

items.q: The difference between an ML model and an ML system is that the ML system:
options: Is the complete ecosystem (data, deployment, monitoring, scaling) around the model
items.explain: An ML model is a mathematical construct that predicts; an ML system is the whole ecosystem — data, deployment, monitoring, scaling (e.g. Apollo integrates many models).

items.q: How does MLOps differ from DevOps?
options: MLOps also versions data and models and adds continuous training/retraining
DevOps versions models, MLOps versions code
items.explain: DevOps versions code and focuses on software deployment; MLOps additionally versions data and models and adds continuous training, validation and retraining.

items.q: In the smart-toaster example, the safest design for the 'max toasting time' guarantee is:
options: Use a non-ML code check and a hardware thermal fuse outside the model
items.explain: ML models are unreliable, so safety comes from layers OUTSIDE the model: a simple non-ML code check plus a hardware thermal fuse — fault-tolerant design that assumes the model can be wrong.

items.q: Guardrails in ML systems primarily protect against:
options: Prompt injection/jailbreaks, adversarial inputs, and PII exposure
items.explain: Guardrails protect against threats like prompt injection/jailbreaks, adversarial inputs that manipulate behavior, and sensitive-information (PII) exposure.

items.q: The input to the implementation phase is the ___, and its output is ___:
items.explain: Implementation takes the design document as input and produces executable software (the input to the testing phase).

items.q: By the slides' naming conventions, classes use ___ and methods use ___:
items.explain: PascalCasing for classes, camelCasing for methods; identifiers should be 2–3 to 30 characters and avoid keyword-like names.

items.q: A 'dangling else' is a problem because:
options: An else could pair with more than one preceding if, causing wrong interpretation
items.explain: A dangling else is an ambiguity where the else could logically pair with more than one if; the compiler pairs it with the nearest if, which may not be intended. Use braces to disambiguate.

items.q: Defensive programming is guided by which principle?
options: Murphy's Law — 'If anything can go wrong, it will'
items.explain: Defensive programming follows Murphy's Law: anticipate and handle potential errors, invalid inputs, and unexpected conditions, including redundant state checks.

items.q: The secure-programming principle that every process should run with the minimum rights needed is:
items.explain: Least Privilege: every process executes with the minimum set of privileges necessary, for the shortest possible time. (Default Deny is about basing access on explicit permission.)

items.q: A test stub is used in top-down testing to:
options: Temporarily replace a called lower-level module, returning fixed values
items.explain: A stub temporarily replaces a called (lower-level) module, returning known fixed values to simulate components not yet integrated (top-down testing). A driver calls the component from above (bottom-up).

items.q: According to the empirical data, design/code inspections detect roughly what fraction of defects vs unit testing (25%)?
options: Exactly the same as unit testing
items.explain: Inspections detect 55–60% of defects vs integration testing 45% and unit testing 25%. After AT&T introduced reviews: +14% productivity, −90% defects.

items.q: A characteristic of STATIC analysis (vs dynamic) is that it:
options: Reasons about all possible paths without execution, but may report false positives
items.explain: Static analysis examines source without execution, reasoning about all paths (may have false positives). Dynamic analysis executes the program — findings are real but limited to what test inputs exercise (false negatives).

items.q: NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter ($327M) was lost due to:
options: An undetected unit mismatch — the kind of bug type/static checking catches
items.explain: The orbiter was lost to an undetected unit mismatch (pound-force vs newton) — exactly the class of defect that stronger typing and static analysis are designed to detect.

items.q: Of the developer's post-coding tasks (build, test, deploy, monitor…), which should be manual?
options: None — automate everything to prevent human error
items.explain: None! Manual processes are error-prone, slow and inconsistent. Automation prevents human errors, ensures repeatability, and catches mistakes before production.

items.q: Build systems determine task order using a:
options: Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of task dependencies
items.explain: Build systems use a DAG so a task runs only after the tasks it depends on finish (e.g. deploy only after build and test), enabling correct, incremental builds.

items.q: A stated disadvantage of continuous integration is that:
options: For very large systems, building and testing on every commit can take a long time
items.explain: CI's con: large systems may take long to build and test on each merge, and if the dev platform differs from the target, system tests may not run in the developer's workspace.

items.q: The four pillars of DevOps are:
items.explain: The four pillars: Collaboration (the heart of DevOps), Affinity (relationships/trust between teams), Tools (automation enablers), and Scaling (org/infra/process/team).

items.q: The difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment is:
options: Delivery keeps software always deployable and releases on demand; Deployment auto-ships every validated change to production with no manual approval
items.explain: Continuous Delivery = always deployable, release on demand (human approves). Continuous Deployment = every validated build auto-deploys to production with no manual gate (needs mature monitoring/rollback).

items.q: DevSecOps is best summarized by which principle?
options: 'Shift left' — integrate security early and continuously across the SDLC
items.explain: DevSecOps 'shifts security left', integrating it at every SDLC phase as a shared responsibility — 'software, safer, sooner' — so weaknesses are found and fixed as code is written.

items.q: Dijkstra's famous statement about testing is that testing can show the:
options: Presence of bugs, but never their absence
items.explain: 'Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence!' — testing finds defects, it cannot prove correctness.

items.q: The 'Pesticide Paradox' principle of testing states that:
options: Repeating the same tests stops finding new bugs — vary the techniques
items.explain: The pesticide paradox: the same tests run repeatedly lose effectiveness as bugs 'adapt'; you must vary/rotate techniques (e.g. add fuzzing, mutation) to find new defects.

items.q: Verification vs validation: 'Are we building the right product?' refers to:
items.explain: Validation = 'building the right product?' (meets user needs). Verification = 'building the product right?' (meets specifications). Mnemonic: V&V = 'Very Very Important'.

items.q: Boundary Value Analysis focuses test cases on:
options: The center of the input range
The boundaries (edges) of input domains, where errors cluster
items.explain: BVA tests the edges (min, max, just-outside) because errors occur more often at boundaries than in the middle. For [1,100]: test 0, 1, 100, 101.

items.q: For a password length valid between 8 and 15, BVA test values would be:
items.explain: BVA tests min−1, min, max, max+1 → 7 (invalid), 8 (valid min), 15 (valid max), 16 (invalid).

items.q: Equivalence Partitioning works on the principle that:
options: If one input in a class works, all should work; if one fails, all fail — so test one per class
items.explain: EP divides the input domain into classes the system treats the same; you test one representative per class. e.g. Age 18–65 → classes <18, 18–65, >65.

items.q: Pairwise (combinatorial) testing reduces test count by ensuring:
options: Every pair of parameter values is covered by at least one test (finds 50–90% of defects)
items.explain: Pairwise testing covers all pairs of parameter values with a minimal test set, catching 50–90% of defects, since most bugs come from one- or two-factor interactions.

items.q: Which test-case type verifies the software does NOT do what it shouldn't (e.g. invalid email → error)?
items.explain: Negative test cases verify the software rejects invalid input/behaviour. Positive verifies correct behaviour; destructive pushes until it breaks (e.g. 1000 logins/sec).

items.q: Cyclomatic complexity V(G) is computed as:
items.explain: V(G) = E − N + 2P (edges − nodes + 2×connected components), equivalently decisions + 1. It equals the number of independent paths / minimum test cases for path coverage.

items.q: A control flow graph with E=8 edges, N=7 nodes, P=1 has cyclomatic complexity:
items.explain: V(G) = 8 − 7 + 2(1) = 3 → three linearly independent paths to test.

items.q: Software reliability is defined as the probability of:
options: Failure-free operation for a specified time in a specified environment
items.explain: Software reliability = probability of failure-free operation over a specified time in a specified environment. Predictive models estimate MTTF; assessment models measure MTBF/failure rate.

items.q: A key advantage of inspections over testing is that:
options: Errors don't mask each other (static), and incomplete systems can be inspected
items.explain: Inspections are static, so errors don't mask one another and incomplete code can be inspected without a test harness; they also check standards/portability. Reviews detect 60–90% of defects.

items.q: Alpha vs beta testing differ in that alpha testing is:
options: Done by external users at their own site
Done by internal/friendly users WITH the dev team at the developer's site
items.explain: Alpha = internal/friendly testers with the dev team at the developer's site (before beta). Beta = external volunteer users in the real environment. Acceptance = customer's go/no-go.

items.q: The main difference between release testing and system testing is that release testing:
options: Is done by the development team to find bugs
Is done by a separate team to validate readiness for external use (a Go/No-Go decision)
items.explain: System testing (dev team) aims to find defects; release testing (separate team) validates the release is good enough for external use, yielding a Go/No-Go decision. Release testing is black-box.

items.q: The golden rule of regression testing is:
options: Re-run all tests on every change; they must pass before committing
items.explain: Regression testing re-runs ALL tests after any change; tests must pass before the change is committed. It's expensive but essential, so it must be automated.

items.q: Soak (endurance) testing is designed to find:
options: Memory leaks, connection leaks, and resource exhaustion over extended runs (8–72h at 70–80% load)
items.explain: Soak testing runs under significant load for an extended period (8–72 hours at 70–80% load) to expose slow-building problems like memory leaks that short tests miss.

items.q: Netflix's Chaos Monkey improves resilience by:
options: Randomly killing production instances (during business hours) to force fault-tolerant design
items.explain: Chaos Monkey randomly terminates AWS instances in production during business hours, forcing resilience by design; the key metric (Stream Starts per Second) stays flat — 99.99% availability by surviving daily chaos.

items.q: Profiling differs from tracing in that profiling:
options: Tracks the call sequence over time
Measures performance to find CPU/memory bottlenecks
items.explain: Profiling analyzes/measures code performance to find CPU/memory bottlenecks; tracing tracks the execution flow and call sequence (useful for deadlocks).

items.q: Mutation testing evaluates the quality of:
options: The test suite — mutants (changed code) should all fail the tests
items.explain: Mutation testing changes (mutates) source statements; a good test suite should 'kill' all mutants (they should fail), proving the tests are robust enough to catch real faults.

items.q: Software Configuration Management primarily provides:
options: Controlled change, traceability, reproducible builds, and concurrent work
items.explain: SCM systematically controls/tracks changes to artifacts (CIs), giving reproducible builds, audit trails/traceability, concurrent work, and controlled change.

items.q: In SCM, which body reviews and approves high-risk changes?
items.explain: The Change Control Board (CCB) reviews high-risk changes and approves/rejects promotions. Other roles: Configuration Manager, Developer, Build/Release Engineer, QA, Auditor.

items.q: A baseline in SCM is:
options: An agreed, frozen snapshot of configuration items
items.explain: A baseline is an agreed, frozen snapshot (functional, development, or release baseline). Changing it requires formal change control. It's the known-good point you can roll back to.

items.q: Semantic versioning uses the format:
items.explain: Semantic versioning = MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for backward-compatible features, PATCH for backward-compatible bug fixes.

items.q: Which branching model uses a single main branch with short-lived feature branches to promote CI?
items.explain: Trunk-based development keeps one main branch + short-lived feature branches, minimizing merge pain and promoting frequent integration. Gitflow uses feature/release/hotfix branches.

items.q: Before approving a change, the CCB weighs all of these EXCEPT:
options: Consequences of not making the change
Number of users affected and the cost
items.explain: The five factors: consequences of not changing, benefits, number of users affected, cost (dev/test/docs/training), and fit with the release cycle. The developer's language preference is irrelevant.

items.q: In the defect lifecycle, a logged bug that is valid but low-priority is marked:
items.explain: During triage a bug can be Rejected (invalid), Duplicate, or Deferred (valid but low priority). Valid bugs go Assigned → In Progress → Fixed → Closed (or Reopened if the fix fails).

items.q: A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is most valuable for:
options: Instantly revealing whether a vulnerable component (e.g. Log4Shell's log4j) is present
items.explain: An SBOM is a machine-readable inventory of all components/versions/licenses. When a CVE like Log4Shell drops, it instantly reveals whether the vulnerable log4j version is present — supply-chain transparency. Standards: SPDX, CycloneDX, SWID.

items.q: Maven differs from Make in that Maven:
options: Uses convention-over-configuration via pom.xml and a standard directory layout (Java)
items.explain: Maven (Java) uses convention-over-configuration with a single pom.xml and standard layout (src/main/java, target/). Make is a general dependency-driven tool using explicit Makefile rules (targets/dependencies/commands).
